Segel has also been in Apatow projects -- including last year's "Forgetting Sarah Marshall" -- and he stars in the TV series "How I Met Your Mother," which finds plenty of humor in male bonding. Segel observes that what helps the films work is the discomfort of two men trying to talk about their emotions while hoping to maintain a dispassionate, hard-edged, prototypically manly façade. And he knows he's good at bringing out that discomfort in his co-stars. "Judd Apatow told me that my special skill was that I am able to maintain my likability while getting incredibly close to the creepy line, and that's what I should try to cultivate," he said. "That's what he does," Rudd noted. "He just holds [the moment] a little too long." "It's the fraction of a second too long that makes people uncomfortable," Segel added. "It was a real treat for me, to be honest for a minute, to play this character, because I've played sort of a puppy dog guy in 'Forgetting Sarah Marshall,' and on ['Mother'] I play a husband, you know, a loving husband," he said. "So to get to play a character who is a bit more of a man of mystery was very exciting for me." In real life, claims Segel, he even has a man cave. "It's filled with puppets," he said. "And I keep wondering why I don't have a girlfriend. I'm like, 'hey, this is my house; come check it out. This is where I keep my 40 puppets.' ... I think that I have a reputation for being weird because of that." But he quickly turns serious and maintains that "I Love You, Man" does have a message to go along with its comedy. "I think we both had something to learn from each other," he said. "Paul's character had to learn that it's all right to take a little distance from your significant other and have some dude friends and someone to vent to about things you can't necessarily talk about with your girl." "Sometimes buddies hold a mirror up to the way you behave in ways that relationships with the opposite sex don't," Rudd said. "Yeah, and my character had to learn that maybe it's time to grow up a little bit," Segel added. So, this "bromance" thing, allowing a few feelings to show. Perhaps it's not so bad after all? Rudd says that the idea has its upside, despite its name. And he's glad it's been successful. "That's us in a nutshell, not macho, not tough," he said. "I think that we've all been kind of drawn to real stories, you know, characters that hopefully people can relate to and what's funny about just certain insecurites and just certain things in life. "They could easily be dramatic," he pointed out. "Just less fart jokes."

NEW YORK (CNN) — They’ve been dubbed “bromances”: films and television shows centered on deep, nonsexual friendships between two or more men, including movies such as “Pineapple Express” and “The 40-Year-Old Virgin.”

The forthcoming “I Love You, Man,” starring Paul Rudd and Jason Segel and opening Friday, appears to fit the bill. In the film, Rudd plays Peter Klaven, a man who needs a best man for his wedding but has never made any male friends. Enter Segel as Sydney Fife, whom Peter pursues on a series of “man-dates” that ultimately threaten his relationship with his fiancée, played by Rashida Jones.

But don’t call the film a “bromance” in front of Rudd and Segel.

“We hate that word,” Segel told CNN.

“It was not part of the lexicon while we were filming,” Rudd added.

Still, both actors have plenty of experience in the, well, guy-pal genre. Rudd has appeared in several comedies written, directed or produced by Judd Apatow, who is considered one of the leaders of the “bromance” trend, with its softer, more openly emotional male characters.

Segel has also appeared in Apatow projects, including last year’s “Forgetting Sarah Marshall,” and stars in the television series “How I Met Your Mother,” which finds ample humor in male bonding.

Segel observes that part of what makes these films work is the discomfort of two men attempting to discuss their emotions while trying to maintain a dispassionate, hard-edged and prototypically masculine façade. He also knows he has a talent for bringing out that discomfort in his co-stars.

“Judd Apatow told me that my special skill was that I am able to maintain my likability while getting incredibly close to the creepy line, and that’s what I should try to cultivate,” he said.

“That’s what he does,” Rudd noted. “He just holds [the moment] a little too long.”

“It’s the fraction of a second too long that makes people uncomfortable,” Segel added.

In “I Love You, Man,” Segel’s character is rougher and looser than those he plays in “Forgetting Sarah Marshall” and “How I Met Your Mother.” He welcomed the change.

“It was a real treat for me, to be honest for a minute, to play this character, because I’ve played sort of a puppy-dog guy in ‘Forgetting Sarah Marshall,’ and on [‘Mother’] I play a husband—you know, a loving husband,” he said. “So to get to play a character who is a bit more of a man of mystery was very exciting for me.”

In real life, Segel claims, he even has a man cave.

“It’s filled with puppets,” he said. “And I keep wondering why I don’t have a girlfriend. I’m like, ‘Hey, this is my house; come check it out. This is where I keep my 40 puppets.’ ... I think that I have a reputation for being weird because of that.”

But Segel quickly turns serious, maintaining that “I Love You, Man” has a message to accompany its comedy.

“I think we both had something to learn from each other,” he said. “Paul’s character had to learn that it’s all right to take a little distance from your significant other and have some dude friends and someone to vent to about things you can’t necessarily talk about with your girl.”

“Sometimes buddies hold a mirror up to the way you behave in ways that relationships with the opposite sex don’t,” Rudd said.

“Yeah, and my character had to learn that maybe it’s time to grow up a little bit,” Segel added.

So perhaps this “bromance” idea—allowing a few feelings to show—isn’t so bad after all. Rudd says the concept has its advantages, despite the name, and he is pleased by its success.

“That’s us in a nutshell: not macho, not tough,” he said. “I think that we’ve all been kind of drawn to real stories—you know, characters that hopefully people can relate to—and what’s funny about just certain insecurities and just certain things in life.

“They could easily be dramatic,” he pointed out. “Just less fart jokes.”

“We hate that word,” Segel told CNN.

Rudd pointed out that the term had not yet entered their vocabulary when the film was being made.

Despite their dislike of the label, both performers are veterans of comedies about male friendship. Rudd has appeared in several projects written, directed, or produced by Judd Apatow, who is regarded as a major force behind the trend because his male characters tend to be gentler and more emotionally expressive.

Segel has also worked on Apatow productions, including the previous year’s “Forgetting Sarah Marshall.” In addition, he stars in the television comedy “How I Met Your Mother,” which frequently finds laughs in relationships between men.

According to Segel, much of the humor comes from watching men struggle to discuss their feelings while trying to preserve a detached, tough, traditionally masculine exterior. He is also aware that he has a talent for making fellow actors visibly uneasy in such moments.

Segel recalled Apatow telling him that his unusual gift was remaining likable while moving extremely close to being creepy—and that he should continue developing that ability.

Rudd explained that Segel creates the effect by letting a moment continue slightly longer than expected. Segel agreed, saying that the extra fraction of a second is what makes audiences uncomfortable.

In “I Love You, Man,” Segel plays someone wilder and less restrained than his roles in “Forgetting Sarah Marshall” and “How I Met Your Mother,” a departure he enjoyed.

He said it was refreshing to take on the part because his “Sarah Marshall” character was more like an eager puppy, while on “Mother” he plays a devoted husband. The opportunity to portray a more mysterious man was therefore especially exciting.

Segel says that, outside of acting, he even has his own “man cave”—although it is packed with puppets. He joked that he cannot understand why he has no girlfriend after inviting women into a home where he keeps 40 puppets. He believes the collection may have earned him a reputation for being strange.

Even so, Segel emphasized that the movie offers a serious point beneath its comedy. In his view, the two central characters each have something to teach the other.

Peter must discover that it is healthy to spend some time apart from his romantic partner, maintain friendships with other men, and have someone with whom he can discuss matters he may not feel able to share with his fiancée.

Rudd added that male friends can sometimes reflect a person’s behavior back to him in a way that relationships with women do not.

Sydney, meanwhile, has his own lesson to learn: Segel said his character needs to recognize that he may have reached the point when he should become more mature.

So perhaps the kind of male friendship called a “bromance”—one that permits men to reveal some emotion—is not such a bad development. Rudd acknowledged that the concept has benefits, even if he dislikes the word, and said he is pleased that such stories have found an audience.

He described himself and his colleagues as neither macho nor tough. Instead, he said, they are attracted to authentic stories and relatable characters, particularly the humor found in ordinary insecurities and experiences. Paul Rudd plays Peter Klaven, a successful real-estate agent who realizes while preparing for his wedding that he has no close male friend to serve as his best man. Although Peter is comfortable with his fiancée, Zooey, and gets along well with the women in his life, he has never learned how to build or maintain intimate friendships with other men. His attempt to solve the problem leads to a series of painfully awkward “man-dates,” each exposing his uncertainty about masculine social rules.

Peter’s search changes when he meets Sydney Fife, played by Jason Segel. Sydney is spontaneous, candid, and largely unconcerned with social expectations. Where Peter is cautious and self-conscious, Sydney is impulsive and emotionally direct. Their contrasting personalities create much of the film’s comedy, but they also allow the story to explore what male friendship can offer: companionship, honesty, shared enthusiasm, and a space in which both men can behave more freely.

Rudd and Segel’s performances emphasize the tension between vulnerability and the traditional masculine façade. Peter wants connection but lacks the language and confidence to express that desire without embarrassment. He overthinks casual conversations, invents uncomfortable nicknames, and repeatedly undermines himself while trying to appear relaxed. Sydney seems more secure, yet his openness and independence conceal emotional needs of his own. The humor comes not from the idea that men should not care about one another, but from the elaborate ways they avoid admitting that they do.

The film’s “bromance” structure also mirrors the conventions of a romantic comedy. Peter and Sydney meet unexpectedly, grow close through shared experiences, encounter conflict, and eventually reconcile. By placing a male friendship at the center of this familiar narrative, *I Love You, Man* treats platonic intimacy as meaningful rather than trivial. Peter’s relationship with Sydney does not compete with his love for Zooey; instead, it helps him become more emotionally balanced and better able to communicate within all his relationships.

In this sense, the film reflects a broader cultural shift in portrayals of masculinity. Its male characters still enjoy conventionally masculine interests and often hide behind jokes, slang, and exaggerated confidence, but they are also permitted to feel lonely, insecure, affectionate, and dependent on one another. Rudd and Segel use awkwardness to show how difficult emotional openness can be for men who have been taught to keep intimacy at a distance. Beneath the comedy, *I Love You, Man* argues that friendship requires the same honesty, effort, and vulnerability as any other important relationship.

# Paul Rudd and Jason Segel revisit male friendship — and the “bromance” — in ‘I Love You, Man’

**By CNN Entertainment**

When “I Love You, Man” arrived in theaters in 2009, the word “bromance” was becoming a pop-culture shorthand for close friendships between men.

For stars Paul Rudd and Jason Segel, however, the comedy was about something more sincere: the difficulty some men have forming meaningful friendships — and admitting they need them.

Rudd plays Peter Klaven, a successful real estate agent who realizes while planning his wedding that he has no close male friend to serve as his best man. His increasingly awkward search leads him to Sydney Fife, played by Segel, a free-spirited and outspoken man who quickly becomes an important part of Peter’s life.

The film, directed by John Hamburg, builds its comedy around “man dates,” uncomfortable introductions and Peter’s painfully unsuccessful attempts at casual slang. Beneath those jokes is a story about vulnerability, loneliness and the emotional expectations placed on men.

Rudd and Segel have discussed how the term “bromance” helped audiences quickly understand the movie’s premise, even if it could also make a genuine friendship sound like a novelty. The relationship between Peter and Sydney is not romantic, but the film treats it as consequential: Like any close bond, it requires honesty, boundaries and effort.

That idea was central to the movie’s appeal. Peter is surrounded by people and is preparing to marry Zooey, played by Rashida Jones, yet he is missing a kind of companionship he did not realize he wanted. Sydney, meanwhile, encourages Peter to loosen up, speak more openly and rediscover parts of himself that had been pushed aside.

The friendship also creates tension. As Peter and Sydney become closer, Peter struggles to balance his new connection with his relationship and responsibilities. The resulting conflict gives the comedy an unexpectedly thoughtful question: Why are friendships sometimes treated as less important than romantic relationships, particularly for adult men?

The chemistry between Rudd and Segel helped make that question feel both funny and believable. Rudd’s tightly wound discomfort contrasts with Segel’s relaxed confidence, while their shared willingness to look ridiculous keeps the film from becoming overly sentimental.

More than a decade after its release, “I Love You, Man” remains a defining comedy of the so-called bromance era. But its lasting message is simpler than the label suggests: Men can love their friends, say so out loud and still be themselves.

Or, as Peter Klaven might put it after several failed attempts, friendship deserves more than an awkward nickname.

## Segel and Rudd put friendship first in ‘I Love You, Man’

**LOS ANGELES —** Jason Segel and Paul Rudd may have made one of Hollywood’s defining male-friendship comedies, but there is one label neither is eager to embrace: “bromance.”

The word became nearly unavoidable around the release of *I Love You, Man*, the 2009 comedy in which Rudd plays Peter Klaven, a successful real-estate agent who realizes he has no close male friend to serve as best man at his wedding. His increasingly awkward search leads him to Sydney Fife, Segel’s uninhibited, Rush-loving bachelor.

In interviews about the film, both actors expressed irritation with “bromance,” a term they felt reduced an ordinary friendship between men to a novelty. Their objection also points to the movie’s central idea: Emotional intimacy should not require a special category simply because the people involved are male.

Directed by John Hamburg, *I Love You, Man* builds its humor around Peter’s discomfort with friendship. He is relaxed with women but painfully self-conscious around men, turning a series of potential “man dates” into comic disasters. Sydney appears to be his opposite—casual, outspoken and unconcerned with social rules—but he, too, needs a meaningful connection.

That balance suited Rudd and Segel, whose comedy careers had developed along different but complementary paths.

Rudd first became widely known through *Clueless* before moving steadily into ensemble comedy. Films such as *Anchorman: The Legend of Ron Burgundy*, *The 40-Year-Old Virgin* and *Role Models* established his talent for playing intelligent, likable men whose composure gradually gives way to panic or absurdity. Peter’s painfully invented slang and desperate attempts to appear at ease make full use of that skill.

Segel came from the more emotionally exposed side of comedy. After *Freaks and Geeks*, he became a television regular on *How I Met Your Mother* and wrote and starred in *Forgetting Sarah Marshall*. His characters often combine outsized behavior with an openness that makes the jokes feel personal rather than merely outrageous.

In *I Love You, Man*, Segel’s looseness helps draw Rudd’s tightly wound character out of his shell. Rudd, in turn, gives the film its escalating embarrassment, especially as Peter tries too hard to reproduce Sydney’s confidence. Their chemistry depends less on competition than on generosity: Each actor leaves room for the other to be ridiculous.

The movie also resists presenting male friendship as an escape from adult commitment. Peter’s fiancée, Zooey, played by Rashida Jones, is not the obstacle to his happiness. She is the person who recognizes that something is missing from his life. The conflict comes when Peter struggles to make room for both romance and friendship without neglecting either.

Beneath the crude jokes, awkward silences and air-guitar sessions, the film argues that men need friends with whom they can be honest, affectionate and vulnerable. It also suggests that finding such a relationship can be as uncertain—and as consequential—as dating.

That message is why the “bromance” description never quite fits. *I Love You, Man* is not treating friendship as a lesser version of romance or as an embarrassing comic substitute. It is presenting friendship as its own essential bond.

For Segel and Rudd, the comedy comes from how difficult men can make that simple truth look.

## Paul Rudd and Jason Segel make the “bromance” a leading man

In *I Love You, Man*, Paul Rudd faces a romantic-comedy dilemma that has little to do with winning the girl.

His character, Peter Klaven, already has the fiancée, the wedding plans and the aggressively pleasant manners. What he does not have is a best man—or, apparently, a close male friend of any kind.

Enter Jason Segel’s Sydney Fife, a laid-back bachelor who treats honesty as a contact sport and lives in a man cave filled with instruments, collectibles and enough puppets to suggest that the Muppets have opened an off-site storage facility.

The comedy arrives as Hollywood is increasingly turning male friendship into a central love story—minus the candlelit dinner, plus more awkward nicknames and arguments about Rush. Films such as *Superbad*, *Pineapple Express* and *Step Brothers* have helped transform the “bromance” from comic subplot into a genre of its own.

Rudd is particularly suited to the trend. His screen persona combines suburban respectability with the nervous energy of a man who has just realized everyone else received the social handbook. Peter’s attempts to be casually masculine produce bizarre slang, painful goodbyes and conversations that seem to surprise him as they leave his mouth.

Segel, meanwhile, plays Sydney with his familiar loose-limbed sincerity. His acting style often suggests a very tall man has wandered into the scene, developed strong feelings and decided to explain them before anyone can call security. That openness keeps Sydney from becoming merely the movie’s wild bachelor stereotype.

Together, the actors give the film its central tension: Peter needs Sydney’s spontaneity, while Sydney may need Peter’s stability. Their friendship follows the familiar rhythms of a romantic comedy—an unlikely meeting, a euphoric courtship, jealousy, separation and reconciliation—while Peter’s fiancée, Zooey, played by Rashida Jones, watches her future husband plunge into the surprisingly complicated world of male bonding.

The movie’s humor rests partly on the idea that adult men are often expected to form friendships without ever discussing how those friendships work. Dating has rules, rituals and vocabulary. Making a new male friend after 30 can feel like trying to negotiate a treaty using only sports references and grilled meat.

That anxiety has fueled the rise of bromance comedies. Their heroes may be emotionally stunted, but the films allow them to crave companionship, admit loneliness and even say “I love you”—provided someone makes a joke immediately afterward.

Sydney’s puppet-populated retreat is a fitting symbol for the genre. The man cave is meant to represent untamed masculinity, yet it is decorated like a rehearsal space for an especially eccentric children’s program. Beneath the guitars and bachelor bravado sits something more vulnerable: a grown man who has built an elaborate clubhouse because he still wants someone to come over and play.

In that sense, *I Love You, Man* is less a parody of friendship than an argument for taking it seriously. Its biggest joke may be that male intimacy is treated as embarrassing. Its warmest insight is that embarrassment is often the price of finding it.
